lines.name: Color palette
lines.controls: Which few colours the work is allowed to use, and so what it is recognised by from across a street.

lines.name: Contrast
lines.controls: How far apart the lightest and darkest parts sit, which sets how hard or soft the image hits.

lines.name: Lighting
lines.controls: Where the light comes from and how hard it is, which tells the viewer what kind of moment this is.

lines.name: Texture
lines.controls: What the surface of the image feels like to the eye: rough, slick, printed, dusty.

lines.name: Depth of field
lines.controls: How much of the picture is sharp, which decides what the viewer is allowed to look at.

lines.name: Grade or finish
lines.detail: film emulation, warm vs cool, faded vs punchy
lines.controls: The overall colour treatment laid over the picture after it is shot.

lines.name: Cropping
lines.controls: Where the frame cuts the subject, and what is left for the viewer to finish.

lines.name: Camera angle
lines.controls: Where the camera stands, which makes the subject an equal, a specimen or a giant.

lines.name: Symmetry vs asymmetry
lines.controls: Whether the two halves of the frame mirror each other or pull against each other.

lines.name: Foreground / background
lines.controls: What sits in front and what sits behind, and how the two layers talk.

lines.name: Focal point
lines.controls: The one spot the eye goes to first.

lines.name: Hierarchy of attention
lines.controls: The order in which the viewer reads the parts of the picture.

lines.name: Negative space
lines.controls: How much of the frame is left empty, and what that emptiness says about the subject.

lines.name: Scale
lines.detail: how big or small things feel
lines.controls: How big or small a thing feels next to the things around it.

lines.name: Density vs minimalism
lines.controls: How many things are in the frame at once.

lines.name: Repetition or pattern
lines.controls: What repeats inside one image or across a series, so a viewer who has seen two ads looks for it in the third.

lines.name: Photography vs illustration vs CG
lines.controls: Which medium makes the picture.

lines.name: Stock vs shot
lines.controls: Whether the image is found or made for the job.

lines.name: Real people vs models vs characters
lines.controls: Who the viewer is looking at: someone like them, someone hired to look good, or someone invented.

lines.name: Polished vs raw
lines.controls: How finished the image looks.

lines.name: Literal vs metaphorical
lines.controls: Whether the picture shows the thing itself or shows another thing that stands for it.

lines.name: Close-up vs wide
lines.controls: How near the camera is to the subject.

lines.name: Who's cast
lines.detail: age, look, energy, non-model vs model
lines.controls: Which person carries the message, and what the viewer already thinks about them.

lines.name: Expression and gaze
lines.controls: What the face is doing and where the eyes point.

lines.name: Gesture and body language
lines.controls: What the body says before any copy is read.

lines.name: Movement and direction of talent
lines.controls: How the person moves, and how much of that was told to them.

lines.name: Wardrobe
lines.controls: What people wear.

lines.name: Props
lines.controls: The objects in the scene.

lines.name: Set & location
lines.controls: Where the scene happens, built or found.

lines.name: Era / time period
lines.controls: Which year the scene looks like it belongs to.

lines.name: Cultural references
lines.controls: Which shared stories, symbols or events the scene points at.

lines.name: Typeface
lines.controls: Which letters carry the words, and whether they only inform or also add a feeling.

lines.name: Type hierarchy
lines.controls: Which words are read first, second and last.

lines.name: Type as image vs type as support
lines.controls: Whether the lettering is the picture or sits under one.

lines.name: Copy-driven vs image-driven
lines.controls: Whether the words or the picture carry the message.

lines.name: Alignment
lines.controls: Which edge or axis the type lines up on.

lines.name: Grid vs anti-grid
lines.controls: Whether elements sit on an even structure or are placed off it on purpose.

lines.name: Iconography
lines.controls: Which symbols and marks stand in for ideas.

lines.name: Frames, borders, containers
lines.controls: The shapes that hold content and separate it from the rest.

lines.name: Genre or world you're borrowing from
lines.detail: film noir, 90s skate, editorial fashion, brutalist
lines.controls: Which existing visual world the work borrows its codes from.

lines.name: Era of visual style
lines.controls: Which period of design or image-making the look comes from.

lines.name: Homage vs originality
lines.controls: How openly the work shows where it came from.

lines.name: Pace and timing
lines.controls: How fast things happen and when each beat happens.

lines.name: Hold vs movement
lines.controls: When the frame stays still and when it moves.

lines.name: Ease and weight
lines.controls: How a movement speeds up and slows down, which makes an object feel heavy or light.

lines.name: Transitions vs hard cuts
lines.controls: How one shot hands over to the next.

lines.name: Camera movement
lines.controls: Whether the camera travels, and how.

lines.name: Loops vs linear
lines.controls: Whether the piece repeats or runs once from start to end.

lines.name: Playful vs serious
lines.controls: How much the work jokes.

lines.name: Clean vs chaotic
lines.controls: How ordered the work feels.

lines.name: Intimate vs epic
lines.controls: Whether the work feels like one person's moment or a huge event.

lines.name: Quiet vs loud
lines.controls: How much the work shouts for attention.

lines.name: Aspirational vs relatable
lines.controls: Whether the viewer is shown a life to want or a life they already have.

lines.name: Budget
lines.controls: How much money there is, treated as a choice that shapes the idea.

lines.name: Location
lines.controls: Where the work can be made or placed.

lines.name: Format
lines.controls: The physical or digital form the work has to take.

lines.name: Timeline
lines.controls: How long there is to make it.

lines.name: Platform norms
lines.controls: What people expect to see on the channel, which the work can follow or break.

lines.name: Brand rules worth breaking
lines.controls: Which of the brand's own habits the work drops on purpose.

lines.name: POV
lines.controls: Whose eyes the viewer looks through.

lines.name: Staged vs candid
lines.controls: Whether the scene looks set up or caught.

techniques.name: Scale disparity
techniques.definition: utilizes the contrast of sizes in order to accentuate a message
techniques.plain: Put a very big thing next to a very small thing so the size gap makes the point.

techniques.name: Saturation blocking
techniques.plain: Fill large flat areas with strong colour so each area reads as one block.

techniques.name: Simultaneous contrast
techniques.plain: Two colours placed side by side change how each one looks, so each seems stronger.

techniques.name: Warm and cool split
techniques.plain: Divide the frame into a warm-coloured part and a cool-coloured part to separate two things.

techniques.name: Semantic juxtaposition
techniques.plain: Place two things with different meanings side by side so the gap between them is the message.

techniques.name: Symmetry
techniques.plain: Mirror the two halves of the frame so the eye reads them as one calm whole.

techniques.name: Face schema
techniques.plain: Arrange a few marks like two eyes and a mouth and people see a face.

techniques.name: Visual rhyme
techniques.plain: Two different things share an outline or a colour, so the eye links them.

techniques.name: Common region
techniques.plain: Things placed inside the same boundary are read as belonging together.

techniques.name: Good continuation
techniques.plain: The eye follows a line or curve past a gap and treats the pieces as one path.

techniques.name: Anthropomorphism
techniques.plain: Give an object a body, a face or behaviour so it reads as alive.

techniques.name: Semantic compounding
techniques.plain: Merge two things into a single form so their meanings add up.

techniques.name: Center placement
techniques.plain: Put the subject dead centre so it is seen first.

techniques.name: Leading lines
techniques.plain: Lines in the picture point the eye toward the subject.

techniques.name: Gaze cue
techniques.plain: The viewer looks where the person in the picture is looking.

techniques.name: Size hierarchy
techniques.plain: The biggest element is read first, the smallest last.

techniques.name: Frame within a frame
techniques.definition: turns the portrait into a small stage. Scenes within scenes.
techniques.plain: Use a window, doorway or border inside the picture to hold the subject.

techniques.name: Body vector
techniques.plain: The direction a body points or moves pulls the eye that way.

techniques.name: Reading path
techniques.plain: Lay elements out so the eye passes through them in a set order.

techniques.name: Closure
techniques.plain: Show part of an outline and the viewer's mind finishes the rest.

techniques.name: Forced perspective
techniques.plain: Line up near and far objects so the camera reads them at a false size or distance.

techniques.name: Caricatural exaggeration
techniques.plain: Push one trait far past real so it is read at once.

techniques.name: Form substitution
techniques.definition: Use the shape of one thing to mean something else.
techniques.plain: Swap an expected object for another object with the same outline.

techniques.name: Visual quotation
techniques.definition: references known genres, periods, or pieces of work. It allows the image to stand on the shoulders of its predecessors, as long as that reference is known (at least subconsciously) by the audience.
techniques.plain: Borrow the look of a known genre, period, format or single work so the viewer brings its meaning along.

techniques.name: Pattern break
techniques.plain: Set up a repeat, then change one item so that item stands out.

techniques.name: Occlusion
techniques.plain: Let one thing cover part of another so the viewer fills in what is hidden.

techniques.name: Crop at the edge
techniques.plain: Cut the subject off at the frame so the viewer imagines the part outside it.

techniques.name: Visible facture
techniques.definition: when the process can be seen in the final work ie when the hand of the maker stays present through painted surfaces, grain, brushwork, and constructed scenery
techniques.plain: Leave the marks of how it was made in the finished piece: pen strokes, paint, cut paper, built sets.

techniques.name: Figure-ground reversal
techniques.definition: Turn the subtraction into the subject.
techniques.plain: Make the empty area the thing the viewer reads, in place of the solid one.

techniques.name: Genre quotation
techniques.definition: If your visuals don't mean anything, try genre quotation. Reference something.
techniques.plain: Visual quotation with one variable set: borrow the codes of a whole genre.

techniques.name: Visual literalism
techniques.definition: Visual literalism is about rendering the message as literally as possible. Word for word, what does the phrase or key message itself look like when translated to images?
techniques.plain: Draw the phrase exactly as worded, so a figure of speech becomes a real picture.

techniques.name: Personification
techniques.definition: personification is a different way of abstracting human qualities, literal human, than anthropomorphism
techniques.plain: Cast a real person to stand for a product, a feature or a problem.

techniques.name: Brand mark as a lens
techniques.definition: using a brand mark as a lens rather than a badge. By treating a brand asset as a framing device, you create a visual formula
techniques.plain: Use the logo or another brand asset to frame a subject. His formula: brand mark + subject (+ optional copy).

techniques.name: Visual device
techniques.definition: That's a visual mechanism where you could swap in any brand or theme, and the executions are endless.
techniques.plain: A repeatable picture formula that takes any subject. It is his other name for a visual solution.

techniques.name: Manipulate the medium
techniques.definition: Think how could you manipulate the medium itself.
techniques.plain: Change the billboard, ticket or page itself so the format delivers the message.

techniques.name: Hockney joiner
techniques.definition: a technique where you piece together a scene with separate photographs taken from different vantage points and moments in time. The very point of the technique is they aren't seamless.
techniques.plain: Build one scene from many overlapping photos taken at different moments. Also called panography.

techniques.name: Design through metaphor
techniques.definition: A powerful concept often invokes a feeling rather than a literal image.
techniques.plain: Suggest the idea with colour and pattern and leave the literal picture out.

techniques.name: Shipping the process
techniques.definition: Instead of hiding the effort behind a 'making of' video, bring those glimpses of the practical setup into the final execution.
techniques.plain: Leave the rigs, crew and mistakes in the final film so people believe it was done for real.

techniques.name: Visual lineage
techniques.definition: Every visual idea carries baggage/associations, references, predecessors. And as art directors, we have a choice: we can utilize parts of that lineage intentionally, or we can accidentally plagiarize it.
techniques.plain: Trace a look back to who did it first, then borrow from further back than everyone else.

techniques.name: Undercranking
techniques.plain: Film at a low frame rate so the action plays back fast and jerky, like silent film.

techniques.name: Hidden jump cut
techniques.plain: Cut inside what looks like one shot so something changes without a visible edit.

techniques.name: Practical lighting
techniques.definition: the lights existing inside the frame
techniques.plain: Light the scene with lamps the viewer can see in the shot, and treat those lamps as props.

techniques.name: The Mismatch
techniques.definition: you've got serene calm footage try pairing that with an aggressive track underneath when the music fights what you're seeing your brain goes 'wait what?'
techniques.plain: Put music under the picture that fights its mood, so the viewer stops to work out why.

techniques.name: The Amplifier
techniques.definition: taking whatever emotion is already on screen and turning up the volume on it
techniques.plain: Pick music with the same mood as the picture so the feeling hits harder.

techniques.name: The Sonic Signature
techniques.definition: repeat these musical motifs in more than just a single video… you're training them to associate a sound with the value you bring
techniques.plain: Reuse the same sound or artist across pieces so people link it to you.

frameworks.name: The Big Idea Pyramid

parts.name: Insight
parts.text: The point at the top, the smallest part. One focused human truth. "People think X, but the reality is Y."

parts.name: Idea
parts.text: The middle band. What you do with that truth, written as a verb. He calls it the creative formula.

parts.name: Execution
parts.text: The wide base, "the largest part of the triangle cuz it has the most detail". The art direction ingredients live here.

frameworks.note: He also calls it "my big idea triangle". Look and feel "can sort of fit between idea and execution" (Short MhMhug5xo9E). NotebookLM drew it upside down; his slide and Short put Insight at the point.

frameworks.name: Idea Sizing Chart

parts.name: Business Strategy & Positioning
parts.text: Row 1, the biggest.

parts.name: Branding
parts.text: Row 2. "Just Do It" grew into this row: "it's larger than a platform".

parts.name: Platform
parts.text: Row 3. The group label "Big Ideas" sits beside this row. Snickers "You're Not You When You're Hungry" is his standard platform.

parts.name: Campaign
parts.text: Row 4. Nike "Rip the Script" is a campaign and a big idea in his telling.

parts.name: Execution
parts.text: Row 5. "what if we just put a sneaker in Time Square well that's not really a big idea that's just coming up with an execution".

parts.name: One-off
parts.text: Row 6. The group label "Small Ideas" sits beside this row.

parts.name: Tactics
parts.text: Row 7.

parts.name: Crap
parts.text: Row 8. Group label "No ideas".

frameworks.note: Eight rows read off the 2026 FigJam board. The three group labels sit in a merged left column, so which rows each label spans is not certain. The 2025 board read Execution twice and had no Tactics row.

frameworks.name: Visual Feeling ↔ Visual Solution

parts.name: Visual Feeling
parts.text: Left end. Copy, dialogue or voice-over tells the message and the visual choices support it. He also says "look and feel". Polaroid, Oatly, Diesel, Arc'teryx Playdate.

parts.name: Middle
parts.text: EF Tours "Later Is Now": "somewhere in between creating the feeling but also the medium itself".

parts.name: Visual Solution
parts.text: Right end. The pairing of images or symbols is the message and copy shrinks to a button. He also says "visual device". LEGO, WMF, Twitter.

frameworks.note: One line with five ticks. Nothing is drawn on it; he places each ad in speech. "There is no right or wrong".

frameworks.name: The three levels of expressing taste

parts.name: Level 1: like or dislike
parts.text: Know what you like and what you reject, on purpose.

parts.name: Level 2: how it feels
parts.text: Say the feeling with a simile, metaphor or reference: "this maybe feels like a Michel Gondry film".

parts.name: Level 3: the ingredients
parts.text: Name what made it feel that way: "the actual ingredients the techniques elements or mediums". "You're filling a pantry."

frameworks.note: His iPad drawing stacks INPUTS, LIKE?, FEELINGS, INGREDIENTS, widest at the bottom.

frameworks.name: The three milestones to unlock taste

parts.name: 1. Broaden your inputs
parts.text: Raise the volume and the variety of what you look at, and capture it. "nobody trusts the taste of someone who only eats fast food".

parts.name: 2. Express your taste
parts.text: Move from liking to feeling to ingredients (the three levels).

parts.name: 3. Become visually literate through immersion
parts.text: Go to the source: photographer portfolios, their reps, agency sites. "the best chefs don't just like sushi they move to japan".

frameworks.note: He says "milestones or techniques" at the start and "three tools" in the recap.

frameworks.name: The five taste types

parts.name: Mainstream taste
parts.text: "Casts the widest net. It's a safe taste." Its use is scale.

parts.name: Cultural taste
parts.text: "Gatekept by lived experience." "you can't claim it if you didn't live it".

parts.name: Counter taste
parts.text: "developed through conviction, the willingness to reject what everyone else wants".

parts.name: Elite taste
parts.text: Judgments where "the criteria is gatekept by pure access or privilege".

parts.name: Commercial taste
parts.text: "a little flavor of aspiration mixed with something familiar and inviting", used to fit a business objective.

frameworks.note: He calls the set "a nuanced matrix of flavor profiles". No chart is drawn on screen.

frameworks.name: Portfolio project types

parts.name: 360 Campaign
parts.text: 1-2. Spec, branded. "Show that your idea 'has legs'. Try for 4-10 different touch-points".

parts.name: Passion Project
parts.text: 1-2. Preferably not branded. "Show who YOU are outside of advertising."

parts.name: Craft or Design-focused Project
parts.text: 1. "this is your opportunity to get obsessive".

parts.name: Experimental / Non-traditional
parts.text: 1, optional. "Formats, mediums, or tech used in surprising ways."

parts.name: Social / Content
parts.text: 1, optional. "Show that you are a master of the hook."

parts.name: Stunt / Cultural Response
parts.text: 1, optional. "Ideally do something for real that garners attention."

frameworks.note: Four to six projects in total. His checklist says 4-6+ touchpoints where this table says 4-10.

frameworks.name: Iris: the four groups

parts.name: Differentiate
parts.text: Red. Tell things apart. Scale disparity sits here.

parts.name: Group
parts.text: Blue. Tie things together. Symmetry, Face schema, Visual rhyme.

parts.name: Sequence
parts.text: Yellow. Order the reading. Center placement, Leading lines, Gaze cue.

parts.name: Predict
parts.text: Purple. Set up an expectation. Closure, Form substitution, Visual quotation, Visible facture.

frameworks.note: The four names are on the filter row of his tool. What each group does is inferred from its name and its techniques; he has published no legend. 39 techniques exist, 28 are read, 11 are unread.
